# Transport You Can Compute: Histograms, Flows, and the Price of Moving Mass {.unnumbered}

*A standalone tutorial. The transport tutorials so far have been about the
continuum — [the intuitive story](./05-transport-story.qmd) and
[the rigorous account](./10-transport-rigorous.qmd). This one puts transport on a
finite ground set, where it becomes a linear program you can solve exactly, and
where the one modelling decision that drives everything — **what does it cost to
move mass?** — is out in the open. Earth Mover's Distance, Word Mover's Distance,
and the Wasserstein distances in generative modelling are all this one problem.
The closing section answers the question this setting always provokes: when the
bins dissolve into a continuous density and the Jacobian shows up, what plays the
role of the cost, and what plays the role of the transporter?*

## 1. Two histograms, one question

Fix four bins $A, B, C, D$ — they can be greyscale levels, vocabulary items,
mesh cells, cluster centroids, anything. Put two probability mass functions on
them:

$$
p = (p_A, p_B, p_C, p_D), \qquad q = (q_A, q_B, q_C, q_D),
\qquad \textstyle\sum_i p_i = \sum_j q_j = 1 .
$$

Now ask how to turn $p$ into $q$ by *moving mass around*. A **transport plan** is
a table $\gamma_{ij} \ge 0$ recording how much mass travels from bin $i$ to bin
$j$, and it is a legal plan exactly when nothing is created or destroyed:

$$
\underbrace{\sum_j \gamma_{ij} = p_i}_{\text{all of bin } i \text{ leaves}},
\qquad
\underbrace{\sum_i \gamma_{ij} = q_j}_{\text{bin } j \text{ receives exactly } q_j} .
$$

::: {.callout-tip}

## You have already met this object

Those two conditions say the non-negative table $\gamma$ has row sums $p$ and
column sums $q$ — that is, **$\gamma$ is a joint distribution whose two marginals
are $p$ and $q$**. A transport plan *is* a coupling, in the exact sense of
[Joint, Marginal, Conditional](./02-joint-conditional-bayes.qmd): the mountain
whose two shadows are $p$ and $q$.

So everything from that tutorial applies verbatim, including the part that
matters most here: **there are many couplings.** The shadows do not determine the
mountain, so the constraints alone do not determine the plan. Something else has
to choose, and that something is the cost.

:::

The set of legal plans is never empty — the **independent coupling**
$\gamma_{ij} = p_i q_j$ always qualifies — and it is a convex polytope, the
*transportation polytope*. Optimal transport is the problem of picking the
cheapest point in it.

## 2. The linear program, and why it is a flow

Let $C_{ij} \ge 0$ be the price of moving one unit of mass from bin $i$ to bin
$j$. Then the total bill for a plan is $\langle \gamma, C\rangle = \sum_{ij}
\gamma_{ij} C_{ij}$, and the **Kantorovich problem** is

$$
\operatorname{OT}_C(p,q) \;=\; \min_{\gamma \ge 0}\; \sum_{i,j} \gamma_{ij} C_{ij}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
\sum_j \gamma_{ij} = p_i, \;\; \sum_i \gamma_{ij} = q_j .
$$

Linear objective, linear constraints, non-negative variables: a linear program.
But it is a linear program of a very particular kind. Draw the bins twice — once
as sources, once as sinks — and join every source to every sink. Then $\gamma$ is
a **flow** on that bipartite graph: $p_i$ is supply at source $i$, $q_j$ is demand
at sink $j$, $C_{ij}$ is the per-unit cost on edge $i \to j$, and we want the
cheapest flow meeting all demands. This is the classical **transportation
problem**, and it is solved by min-cost-flow machinery — network simplex, the
Hungarian algorithm in the assignment special case, auction algorithms —
rather than by a general-purpose LP solver.

Two structural facts are worth carrying around.

**Sparsity.** The constraint matrix here is totally unimodular, and a vertex
(basic feasible solution) of an $m \times n$ transportation polytope has at most
$m + n - 1$ non-zero entries. For our $4 \times 4$ problem that is **7 of the 16
routes**. An optimal plan is always sparse: most pairs of bins never trade. The
demo below shows the count live.

**Duality, as prices.** The dual of the program above is

$$
\max_{f, g} \;\; \sum_i f_i\, p_i + \sum_j g_j\, q_j
\qquad \text{subject to} \qquad f_i + g_j \le C_{ij} \;\; \text{for all } i,j,
$$

which has an irresistible reading. Imagine a shipping contractor who offers to
collect a unit at bin $i$ for a fee $f_i$ and deliver it at bin $j$ for $g_j$.
The constraint says the contractor can never charge more than it would cost you
to move the mass yourself. Duality says that, at the optimum, the contractor's
best total take equals your cheapest shipping bill exactly. When $C$ is a metric
this specialises to the **Kantorovich–Rubinstein** form, $\operatorname{OT}_C =
\sup_{\text{1-Lipschitz } f} \sum_i f_i (p_i - q_i)$ — the form a Wasserstein GAN
critic approximates.

## 3. The cost function is the modelling decision

Here is the point of the whole tutorial. The bins, the histograms, and the
constraints are fixed. Change only the price list $C$ and you get a different
optimal plan, a different total, and — this is the part that surprises people —
a different *kind of geometry* on the space of histograms.

Four price lists, all built from the bin index distance $d = |i-j|$:

| $C_{ij}$ | Name | Optimal total is | Plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\lvert i - j\rvert$ | distance on a line | $W_1$, the **Earth Mover's Distance** | monotone |
| $(i-j)^2$ | squared distance | $W_2^2$ (its square root is $W_2$) | monotone |
| $\mathbf{1}[i \ne j]$ | all-or-nothing | the **total variation distance** | typically not monotone |
| $\sqrt{\lvert i-j \rvert}$ | concave in distance | no standard name | mass prefers to stay put |

Three of these deserve a proof sketch, because each is a small surprise.

**All-or-nothing gives total variation.** If every move costs the same regardless
of distance, the only thing worth optimising is *how much you move at all*. You
can leave $\min(p_i, q_i)$ in place in each bin, and everything else must move,
so

$$
\operatorname{OT}_{\mathbf{1}[i \ne j]}(p,q)
= 1 - \sum_i \min(p_i, q_i)
= \tfrac12 \sum_i |p_i - q_i|
= \mathrm{TV}(p,q).
$$

Total variation is optimal transport with a cost that has no sense of distance —
which is exactly why TV is so brutal a distance between distributions with
disjoint supports, and why generative modelling reaches for Wasserstein instead.

**Distance-on-a-line gives the area between the CDFs.** With bins ordered on a
line, the optimum is the monotone (quantile) coupling, and

$$
W_1(p,q) \;=\; \sum_{k} \big| F_p(k) - F_q(k) \big| ,
$$

the total gap between the two cumulative distributions. This is the discrete
image of the inverse-CDF transport that
[The Map, Proved](./08-map-proved.qmd) builds in the continuum: the same map, on
a finite ground set.

**Convex costs never cross; concave costs do.** For any cost $c(|i-j|)$ with $c$
*convex*, the monotone coupling is optimal — mass keeps its order, and in the
ribbon picture no ribbon crosses another. For $c$ *concave*, the structure flips:
moving one unit a long way is cheaper than moving two units half as far, so the
optimal plan leaves common mass untouched and ships the residue in long jumps.
The plans genuinely differ; the demo flags which case you are in.

::: {.callout-warning}

## When is the answer a distance?

Not always. If $C$ is itself a metric on the ground set ($C_{ii}=0$, symmetric,
triangle inequality), then $\operatorname{OT}_C$ is a metric on the simplex of
histograms — this is the $W_1$/EMD case, and it is what earns EMD the word
"distance." Drop any of those conditions and you may keep a useful number while
losing the guarantees: $(i-j)^2$ is *not* a metric on bins, and correspondingly
$W_2^2$ does not satisfy the triangle inequality — only its square root $W_2$
does. A cost with $C_{ii} \neq 0$ will not even vanish when $p = q$.

The demo reports totals under all four price lists at once. Their **magnitudes
are not comparable** — different units, and scaling $C$ scales the answer.
What is comparable is the plan each induces and the ordering each imposes on
pairs of histograms.

## 4. Plans versus maps: Kantorovich versus Monge

Monge asked the question first, in 1781, and asked a harder version of it. He
wanted a **map**: a rule $T$ sending each source location to a single destination,
with total cost $\sum_i p_i\, C_{i, T(i)}$. Kantorovich's 1942 relaxation allows
mass at one location to *split* across several destinations — that is what the
table $\gamma$ permits and a function $T$ does not.

The relaxation is not a technicality; without it the problem can have no solution
at all. Take $p = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0, 0)$ and $q = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13,
\tfrac13, 0)$. No map works: bin $A$ holds mass $\tfrac12$, every target bin wants
at most $\tfrac13$, so $A$'s mass *must* be split. A plan handles this without
comment; a map cannot exist.

This is the discrete shadow of the atomic obstruction in
[Generative Models as Transport](./10-transport-rigorous.qmd): a deterministic
map cannot split an atom. Generation *into* an atomic target is always fine;
deterministic encoding *out of* an atomic source is what fails. Kantorovich's
plans are the repair, and they are why the modern theory is stated in terms of
couplings rather than maps.

## 5. From bins to densities: what replaces the cost, and the transporter

Now let the bins dissolve. Replace the finite ground set by $\mathbb{R}^d$, the
histograms by densities $p$ and $q$, and ask the same question. A natural first
thought is that the change-of-variables formula is what defines transport here:
if $T$ is a smooth invertible map pushing $p$ onto $q$, then

$$
p(x) \;=\; q\big(T(x)\big)\, \big|\det \nabla T(x)\big| .
$$

That formula is indeed central — but it is worth being precise about *which* role
it plays, because this is the most common confusion in the subject.

::: {.callout-important}

## The Jacobian is the constraint, not the cost

Look back at §1. The discrete problem had two separate ingredients:

1. **Constraints** — row sums $p$, column sums $q$: "$\gamma$ is a coupling."
2. **Objective** — $\sum \gamma_{ij} C_{ij}$: "and it is the cheapest one."

In the continuum the Jacobian equation above is ingredient **1**, and nothing
else. It is precisely the statement $T_\# p = q$ — *this map is a valid
transport* — written in densities. It is the continuous form of "the row sums and
column sums come out right."

It says nothing whatever about cost. Just as infinitely many couplings satisfy
the marginal constraints, infinitely many maps satisfy the Jacobian equation, and
the Jacobian cannot prefer one to another. You still need to name a price.

:::

So the dictionary is:

| Discrete (this tutorial) | Continuous, static | Continuous, dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| bins $i, j$ | points $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^d$ | a path of densities $p_t$ |
| $p_i$, $q_j$ | densities $p$, $q$ | endpoints $p_0 = p$, $p_1 = q$ |
| plan $\gamma_{ij} \ge 0$ | coupling measure $\gamma(dx,dy)$ | velocity field $v_t(x)$ |
| row/column sums | $T_\# p = q$, i.e. the **Jacobian equation** | **continuity equation** $\partial_t p_t + \nabla\!\cdot(p_t v_t) = 0$ |
| cost matrix $C_{ij}$ | cost function $c(x,y)$ | kinetic energy density $\lVert v_t(x)\rVert^2$ |
| $\sum_{ij}\gamma_{ij}C_{ij}$ | $\iint c(x,y)\, d\gamma$ | $\int_0^1\!\!\int \lVert v_t\rVert^2 p_t \,dx\,dt$ |
| min-cost flow | Monge–Kantorovich problem | Benamou–Brenier problem |

Three consequences, all of them load-bearing for this course.

**The transporter is a velocity field.** In the dynamic (Benamou–Brenier) form,

$$
W_2^2(p,q) \;=\; \min_{(p_t, v_t)} \int_0^1\!\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}
\lVert v_t(x)\rVert^2 \, p_t(x)\,dx\,dt
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\partial_t p_t + \nabla\!\cdot(p_t v_t) = 0,
$$

the unknown is not a matrix and not a map but a **time-dependent vector field**;
the map is recovered as the flow of that field. The continuity equation is the
*infinitesimal* Jacobian equation — along a trajectory $\dot\Phi_t = v_t(\Phi_t)$,
the Jacobian obeys $\frac{d}{dt}\log\det\nabla\Phi_t = (\nabla\!\cdot v_t)\circ
\Phi_t$, which is the same bookkeeping in derivative form. This is exactly the
object that flow matching regresses onto and that the
[probability-flow ODE](./09-probability-flow-ode.qmd) integrates. *Learning a
velocity field is learning a transporter*, and the kinetic energy is its cost.

**Quadratic cost has a canonical answer.** For $c(x,y) = \tfrac12\lVert
x-y\rVert^2$, Brenier's theorem (1991) says the optimal map is the gradient of a
convex function, $T = \nabla\varphi$. Substituting into the Jacobian equation
gives the **Monge–Ampère equation**

$$
p(x) \;=\; q\big(\nabla\varphi(x)\big)\, \det\big(\nabla^2\varphi(x)\big),
$$

the constraint and the cost finally in one place. Note what each contributed: the
Jacobian equation supplied the equation, and the cost supplied the restriction to
*gradients of convex functions* — the higher-dimensional replacement for
"monotone," and the reason $W_2$ generalises the quantile map.

**Maximum likelihood is not a transport cost.** A normalizing flow trains on

$$
\log p_{\text{model}}(x) = \log q\big(T(x)\big) + \log\big|\det \nabla T(x)\big| ,
$$

and the Jacobian term sits squarely in the *objective* — which invites the
reading that flows are doing optimal transport. They are not. That term is
enforcing normalization, i.e. the constraint; it does not price displacement. Two
maps $T$ and $T \circ S$, where $S$ is any map preserving $p$, push $p$ to the
same $q$ and are worth exactly the same likelihood, while having wildly different
transport costs. Maximum likelihood identifies the *density*; it does not select
a map. To get the optimal map you have to add a transport cost on purpose — which
is what OT-regularised flows and minibatch-OT couplings in flow matching do, and
why they straighten trajectories that likelihood training leaves tangled.

## 6. Computing it, at realistic sizes

The $4 \times 4$ lab is solved exactly by min-cost flow. Real problems are bigger,
and three routes matter.

- **Network simplex / Hungarian.** Exact, and the right answer for moderate $n$.
  Roughly $O(n^3 \log n)$ for the transportation problem; the Hungarian algorithm
  is the $O(n^3)$ special case when both histograms are uniform with equal atoms,
  so the plan is a permutation.
- **Entropic regularisation (Sinkhorn).** Add $\varepsilon \sum_{ij}\gamma_{ij}
  (\log \gamma_{ij} - 1)$ to the objective. The problem becomes strictly convex,
  and its solution has the form $\gamma = \operatorname{diag}(u)\, K
  \operatorname{diag}(v)$ with $K = e^{-C/\varepsilon}$, found by alternately
  rescaling rows and columns. Each iteration is a matrix–vector product: $O(n^2)$,
  GPU-friendly, and differentiable, which is why it dominates in machine learning
  (Cuturi, 2013). The regulariser interpolates between the two couplings we have
  already met: as $\varepsilon \to 0$ it recovers the sharp optimal plan, and as
  $\varepsilon \to \infty$ it relaxes to the independent coupling $p q^{\top}$ —
  the "shipping blind" baseline reported in the demo.
- **Sliced and low-rank approximations.** Project to one dimension, where the
  answer is the sorted-order formula of §3, and average over projections. Cheap,
  and exact in the only dimension where transport is exactly solvable — which is
  the same reason this course starts in 1-D.

## 7. Where this shows up

- **Earth Mover's Distance.** Rubner, Tomasi and Guibas introduced EMD for image
  retrieval: represent an image by a signature of colour clusters, let $C$ be
  distance in colour space, and compare images by transport cost. Robust to the
  binning artefacts that wreck bin-by-bin distances like $\chi^2$ — because EMD
  knows that adjacent bins are *nearly the same*, and TV does not.
- **Word Mover's Distance.** Kusner and coauthors applied the same idea to text:
  a document is a histogram over its vocabulary, and $C_{ij}$ is the Euclidean
  distance between word embeddings $i$ and $j$. Document distance is then the
  cheapest way to transport one bag of words onto another. This is the
  "fixed vocabulary on both sides" setting exactly — and it shows what the cost
  matrix buys you: semantics enters *only* through $C$.
- **Generative modelling.** Wasserstein GANs optimise the dual form of $W_1$ with
  a Lipschitz-constrained critic. FID scores samples with a closed-form $W_2$
  between Gaussians fitted to Inception features. Minibatch-OT couplings in flow
  matching pick which noise sample is paired with which data sample, straightening
  the paths a model has to learn. And the course's central claim — generative
  modelling *is* transport — is the statement that all of these are choosing a
  coupling between a simple distribution and a complicated one.

::: {.callout-tip}

## Key takeaway

Transport has two ingredients and they do different jobs. The **constraints** say
which plans are legal: row and column sums on a finite ground set, the Jacobian
equation for a map between densities, the continuity equation for a flow. They
never single out an answer, because couplings are plentiful — the lesson of
[many mountains, same shadows](./02-joint-conditional-bayes.qmd). The **cost**
is what selects, and it is a modelling choice, not a mathematical given. Choose
$\mathbf{1}[i \ne j]$ and you have total variation; choose $|i-j|$ and you have
Earth Mover; choose embedding distance and you have Word Mover; choose
$\lVert v\rVert^2$ along a path and you have the velocity field this course
spends the rest of its time learning.

:::

## Exercises

1. Verify the total-variation identity directly: show
   $1 - \sum_i \min(p_i,q_i) = \tfrac12\sum_i |p_i - q_i|$ for any two PMFs, and
   explain why the plan "leave $\min(p_i,q_i)$ in place" is optimal for the
   all-or-nothing cost. Confirm against the demo's readout.
2. Take $p = (0.4, 0.1, 0.1, 0.4)$ and $q = (0.1, 0.4, 0.4, 0.1)$. Compute the
   optimal plan and cost by hand for $C_{ij} = |i-j|$, using the CDF formula.
   Then predict, before clicking, which routes the demo will use.
3. Show that the independent coupling $\gamma_{ij} = p_i q_j$ is always feasible,
   and give an example where it is also *optimal*. (What must $C$ look like?)
4. Prove that a vertex of the $m \times n$ transportation polytope has at most
   $m + n - 1$ non-zero entries. *(Hint: a cycle among the used routes lets you
   push mass around it in either direction at no change to the marginals.)*
5. Exhibit two histograms and a cost $C$ with $C_{ii} = 0$ and symmetry but
   *violating* the triangle inequality, such that $\operatorname{OT}_C$ violates
   the triangle inequality on histograms. Then explain why $W_2^2$ is not a
   metric but $W_2$ is.
6. *(Concave costs.)* With $C_{ij} = \sqrt{|i-j|}$, find $p, q$ for which the
   optimal plan is **not** monotone, and describe in words what the optimal plan
   prefers to do instead. Why does convexity of $c$ rule this out?
7. *(The Jacobian is not the cost.)* Let $p = q = \mathcal{N}(0, I_2)$ on
   $\mathbb{R}^2$. Show that both $T = \mathrm{id}$ and $T = R_\theta$, any
   rotation, satisfy the change-of-variables equation and push $p$ to $q$.
   Compute the quadratic transport cost of each. Which does maximum likelihood
   prefer, and which does optimal transport prefer?
8. *(Dynamic form.)* For $p = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $q = \mathcal{N}(\mu, 1)$ in
   one dimension, guess the optimal velocity field $v_t$, verify it satisfies the
   continuity equation, and compute its kinetic energy. Check the total against
   $W_2^2 = \mu^2$.
